docs.title: Kepos
docs.text:
A community-maintained collection of graduate program experiences — syllabi, course notes, reading lists, and application experiences — aimed primarily at Iranian students considering or currently in Master's/PhD programs abroad.

Named for Epicurus's Kepos ("The Garden"), a school unusually open to outsiders for its time. The goal here is similar: a space that grows as contributors from different programs and universities add their own experience.

• Universities — program overviews, course notes, and session-by-session content, organized by university → semester → course.

docs.title: Admission requirements
docs.text: An undergraduate degree in philosophy or a related field (physics, chemistry, biology, astronomy, mathematics, political science, sociology, psychology, historiography, or economics). A selection committee evaluates whether a given degree qualifies.

docs.title: Program focus
docs.text:
Centers on critical reflection on the sciences, with focus areas in ethics and epistemology of the natural sciences, life sciences, humanities, and social sciences. Coursework spans metaphysics, epistemology, philosophy of mind, and moral/political philosophy, plus elective modules in specialized areas.

The program and the Institute of Philosophy as a whole put particular weight on values in science: how ethical, social, and political values shape (and should shape) scientific research, and what that means for the credibility of scientific knowledge. Expect this theme to run through many courses rather than sit in a single module.

docs.title: SOCRATES center
docs.text: Closely tied to this focus is SOCRATES (Social Credibility and Trustworthiness of Expert Knowledge and Science-Based Information), a DFG-funded Centre for Advanced Studies based at the Institute of Philosophy at LUH. It runs an interdisciplinary forum on scientific credibility and public trust in science, with a seminar series, events, and summer schools (e.g. one on trust, values, and uncertainty in climate action). It is a research center rather than a degree program, so check its site for which events are open to students.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: An introduction to the formal, statistical, and mathematical tools that show up increasingly in contemporary philosophy of science, aimed at building enough literacy to critically engage with research that uses them. Covers formal logic, probability theory, Bayesian approaches to scientific reasoning, and the basics of decision and game theory — and how each shapes current debates in philosophy of science.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of the course, students should:

  1. Be familiar with some of the core formal methods used in philosophy of science.
  2. Have a basic understanding of how those methods are used in the field.
  3. Be able to apply basic formal techniques to analyze and solve selected problems in philosophy of science.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A survey of classic and contemporary answers to core questions in ethics: what makes a good life, how we should act toward others, what makes an action right or wrong, and when we're obliged to help. Moves from ancient sources (Epicurus, Plato, Aristotle) through early modern and modern moral theory (Hobbes, Mill, Kant) to contemporary applied ethics (Peter Singer, Judith Jarvis Thomson), using challenging cases and thought experiments throughout.

docs.title: Session 1: Preliminaries and Introduction
docs.text: Course conception, topic, scope, schedule, and requirements. No coursework for this session — students are asked to come having thought about their own starting assumptions about the good life, how we should conduct ourselves, and how we should treat others.

docs.title: Session 2: What Is the Good Life? The Hedonist's Picture
Required reading
docs.text:
• Shafer-Landau, The Ethical Life, Introduction.
  • Epicurus, Letter to Menoeceus.
  • Mill, John Stuart, Hedonism (course textbook, ch. 1).

docs.title: Discussion focus
docs.text: Epicurus's case against fearing death and his picture of the most pleasant life; Mill's claim that pleasure and freedom from pain are the only things desirable as ends; whether either author's account of a good life is plausible.

docs.title: Session 3: Challenges to Hedonism, Desire Satisfaction Theory
Required reading
docs.text:
• Nozick, Robert, The Experience Machine (course textbook, ch. 2).
  • Heathwood, Chris, Faring Well and Getting What You Want (course textbook, ch. 3).

docs.title: Discussion focus
docs.text: Nozick's experience-machine thought experiment as a challenge to hedonism; whether it refutes hedonism outright; Heathwood's desire-satisfaction account of welfare and possible counterexamples to it.

docs.title: Required reading
docs.text: • Plato, Euthyphro (course textbook, ch. 6).

docs.title: Discussion focus
docs.text: Euthyphro's successive attempts to define piety and why Socrates finds them inadequate; the Euthyphro Question ("is the pious loved by the gods because it is pious, or pious because it is loved by the gods?") and its analogue for monotheistic divine-command theories.

docs.title: Required reading
docs.text: • Aquinas, Thomas, Natural Law (course textbook, ch. 7).

docs.title: Discussion focus
docs.text: What sense of "natural" Aquinas's account of virtue and vice requires; what it means to call natural law a "dictate of practical reason"; whether natural law theory can be defended without depending on divine authorship.

docs.title: Required reading
docs.text:
• Mill, John Stuart, Utilitarianism (course textbook, ch. 8).
  • Williams, Bernard, A Critique of Utilitarianism.

docs.title: Discussion focus
docs.text: Whether utilitarian impartiality really rules out partiality to oneself or family; Mill's claim that virtuous people rarely act with the Greatest Happiness Principle explicitly in mind; whether motive is really irrelevant to an action's morality; Williams's objection to utilitarianism and whether it's a serious problem for the view.

docs.title: Required reading
docs.text: • Kant, Immanuel, The Good Will and the Categorical Imperative (course textbook, ch. 9).

docs.title: Discussion focus
docs.text: What Kant means by calling the good will "good without limitation"; his reasons for denying that happiness is always good; the distinction between acting "in conformity with duty" and acting "from duty," and whether only the latter has moral worth.

docs.title: Required reading
docs.text: • Hobbes, Thomas, Leviathan (course textbook, ch. 10).

docs.title: Discussion focus
docs.text: Hobbes's claim that humans are fundamentally equal; his argument that life without government devolves into a "war of every man against every man"; whether justice and injustice can exist without an authority to enforce them.

docs.title: Session 9: Prima Facie Duties; A Plurality of Moral Rules
Required reading
docs.text: • Ross, W. D., What Makes Right Acts Right (course textbook, ch. 11).

docs.title: Discussion focus
docs.text: Ross's objections to consequentialism and to Kant's exceptionless moral rules; what he means by "prima facie duties" as distinct from "duty proper," and how they're meant to guide action in particular situations.

docs.title: Required reading
docs.text: • Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics (course textbook, ch. 12).

docs.title: Discussion focus
docs.text: Aristotle's distinction between performing virtuous actions and being a virtuous person; virtue as a "mean" between extremes and whether that's consistent with holding some acts always wrong; his advice for finding the mean.

docs.title: Session 11: Metaethics and Skepticism About Objective Morality
Required reading
docs.text: • Hume, David, Moral Distinctions Not Derived From Reason (course textbook, ch. 14).

docs.title: Optional reading
docs.text: • Enoch, David, Why I Am an Objectivist about Ethics (And Why You Are Too) (course textbook, ch. 17).

docs.title: Discussion focus
docs.text: Hume's claim that reason has no influence on our passions and actions, and his argument that moral rules aren't conclusions of reason; whether moral judgments are best explained as products of passion rather than reason.

docs.title: Required reading
docs.text:
• Singer, Peter, The Singer Solution to World Poverty (course textbook, ch. 20).
  • Brennan, Jason, International Aid: Not the Cure You're Hoping For (course textbook, ch. 22).

docs.title: Discussion focus
docs.text: Singer's "Bob and the Bugatti" case and what it's meant to show about our obligations to strangers vs. those we alone can save; whether the difference between Bob's situation and everyday charity is morally relevant; Brennan's institutional-change objection to aid-based solutions.

docs.title: Required reading
docs.text:
• Thomson, Judith Jarvis, A Defense of Abortion (course textbook, ch. 31).
  • Marquis, Don, Why Abortion Is Immoral (course textbook, ch. 32).

docs.title: Discussion focus
docs.text: Thomson's violinist thought experiment and what it does (and doesn't) show about the permissibility of abortion; her account of what a "right to life" amounts to; whether Marquis's criticisms of the standard arguments on both sides succeed.

docs.title: Introduction to Philosophy of Science (Core Course)
Description
docs.text: A survey of central themes in 20th- and 21st-century philosophy of science, moving from logical positivism and Popper's falsificationism through Kuhn's philosophy of science, feminist philosophy of science, and up to current debates on science policy and open science. Recurring topics include explanation, confirmation, reduction, pluralism, values in science, concept formation, models, and experimentation — plus how philosophy of science relates to the history and social study of science.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of the course, students should be able to:

  1. Give a broad overview of topics and debates in 20th/21st century philosophy of science.
  2. Explain key concepts (observation, explanation, values in science, etc.).
  3. Situate those concepts within their major debates (e.g. DN-explanation vs. mechanistic explanation, realism vs. antirealism, value-free vs. value-laden science).
  4. Work with a range of classic and recent texts and authors in the field.
  5. Read and analyze philosophical texts with some competence.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: An introduction to the philosophy (and history) of measurement, built around Hasok Chang's Inventing Temperature: Measurement and Scientific Progress (2004). Central questions: How have measurement standards emerged and evolved? What's the relationship between modeling and measurement? What can and can't be measured? What warrants a claim to an accurate measurement? How can one tell whether an instrument measures what it's meant to measure?

docs.text: Overview of the block seminar's working-group structure (see course overview for details). Groups are assigned a chapter of Chang's Inventing Temperature and split into a historical/narrative subgroup and a philosophical/analysis subgroup, each preparing a presentation and leading discussion of their half of the chapter.

docs.title: Chapter 1 — Keeping the Fixed Points Fixed
docs.text:
• Narrative: What to do when water refuses to boil at the boiling point.
  • Analysis: The meaning and achievement of fixity.

docs.title: Discussion questions
docs.text:
• How were the fixed points (of the boiling and freezing of water) established? What do "superheating"/"supercooling" experiments show about the challenges of fixing those points on the eventual temperature scale?
  • Does Chang succeed in his explication of quantitative measurement (think: ordinal vs. cardinal scale)? Chang follows Middleton's distinction between thermoscopes and thermometers (p. 41): one is "graduated by [...] principles that would give systematic meaning to their readings," the other is not.
  • How does Chang try to justify that numerical thermometers "allowed a true quantification of temperature" (p. 48)? Does the attempt succeed?

docs.title: Chapter 2 — Spirit, Air, and Quicksilver
docs.text:
• Narrative: The search for the "real" scale of temperature.
  • Analysis: Measurement theory in the context of empiricism.

docs.title: Discussion questions
docs.text:
• What is "the problem of nomic measurement"?
  • Did Regnault's criterion of comparability (pp. 59–60, 77, 89) conclusively solve the (nomic) problem of temperature measurement, by showing which thermometric measurement operations are most internally consistent?
  • Chang argues that Regnault's principle of single value "is not an empirical hypothesis" (p. 91) and "can only have a metaphysical justification" (p. 92). Does the argument succeed? Why or why not?

docs.title: Chapter 3 — To Go Beyond
docs.text:
• Narrative: Measuring temperature when thermometers melt and freeze.
  • Analysis: The extension of concepts beyond their birth domains.

docs.title: Discussion questions
docs.text:
• What is "operationalism," and how does it relate to the notion of "validity" (see "The Validation of Standards," pp. 40–44)?
  • How does Chang confront the apparent impossibility of validating measurement methods under Bridgman's operationalism (think: Wittgenstein and "meaning as use," p. 150)?
  • Does Chang's critique of Bridgman's operationalism extend to concepts outside the physical sciences (e.g. the social sciences)? Can you think of examples where it would, or wouldn't, hold?

docs.title: Chapter 4 — Theory, Measurement, and Absolute Temperature
docs.text:
• Narrative: The quest for the theoretical meaning of temperature.
  • Analysis: Operationalization — making contact between thinking and doing.

docs.title: Discussion questions
docs.text:
• Why did William Thomson (Lord Kelvin) conclude that it's unsatisfactory to define temperature relative to a particular substance (e.g. air)?
  • How did Thomson arrive at his preferred definition of "absolute temperature," and what does it entail epistemically (p. 202 ff.)?
  • Did the Joule–Thomson experiment let them correct air thermometers so that air thermometers could measure "absolute temperature"?
  • What are Thomson's three theoretical definitions of temperature grounded in, respectively — and why does the chapter treat the differences between them as irrelevant to his overall concept of temperature?

docs.title: Chapter 5 — Measurement, Justification, and Scientific Progress
Discussion questions
docs.text:
• What's Chang's term for his own philosophical position on measurement and scientific progress?
  • What does that position entail, what view of science does it rely on, and how does Chang defend it?
  • On this picture, how can "scientific progress be measured"?
  • Does Chang's explication of quantitative measurement hold together across the book? Earlier he distinguishes thermoscopes from thermometers by whether they're "graduated by [...] principles that would give systematic meaning to their readings" (p. 41) — i.e. numbers whose arithmetical operations yield meaningful results. On p. 229, he distinguishes ordinal from cardinal quantities instead, which seems to sit awkwardly with reserving "thermometer" for instruments with a quantitative scale determined by an identifiable method (p. 41).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Builds core research, writing, and argumentation skills through short facilitated sessions and small weekly assignments, culminating in a mini-essay and the start of an independent research project.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of the course, students should:

  1. Understand what constitutes a philosophical question and be able to ask one.
  2. Know the basic structure of philosophical texts and be able to identify theses and arguments in them.
  3. Be able to examine and evaluate philosophical arguments (validity and soundness; argument/fallacy types).
  4. Be able to work independently on a philosophical question — literature search, generating and situating questions, using examples, constructing arguments.
  5. Know the formal requirements of academic philosophical work (citation, bibliography, avoiding plagiarism).

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
The seminar moves through three blocks:

  • Block I — Reading and doing philosophy: how to read philosophical texts, identify theses and arguments, and start constructing your own.
  • Block II — Researching and writing a mini-essay: starting a project, structuring a paper, using philosophical tools (examples, test cases, counterexamples), culminating in a mini-essay.
  • Block III — Getting started on your own research project: reflecting on the mini-essay process, referencing/citation practice, and developing the research question for an independent project.

See sessions/ for the week-by-week topics and pre-readings.

docs.title: Writing & exam guidelines
docs.text: Condensed from Prof. Feest's guidance on seminar papers and exam handouts/Thesenpapiere, used across several courses in the program (not a verbatim reproduction — see the original documents for the full text).

docs.title: Seminar papers
docs.text:
• Start from a clearly scoped question. State the topic, question, and goal in the introduction; keep the goal realistic for a seminar paper (e.g. "analyze a specific problem in Kuhn's model," not "develop a theory of scientific development").
  • Have a thesis, usually stated at the end of the introduction. Distinguish an interpretation thesis (your reading of what a text claims) from a discussion thesis (your evaluation of that claim, which can go beyond the text).
  • Substantiate both. For an interpretation thesis, back it with textual evidence (quotes, with page numbers). For a discussion thesis, pinpoint precisely where the problem lies — inconsistency, ambiguous terms, flawed premises, an invalid inference — and explain why. Watch the scope of your own claims: disproving one argument for X doesn't show X is false.
  • Suggested structure: introduction → textual analysis (reconstruct the author's thesis/argument, not a full summary) → discussion (your own thesis, situated against the text) → summary and outlook.
  • Sources: ground your interpretation in primary and secondary literature (encyclopedia overviews like the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy are a good starting point), but always cite — quoted text in quotation marks with a precise reference, paraphrases also referenced. Author–date citation (Chicago style) is the convention in philosophy of science.
  • Formal requirements: cover page (name, matriculation number, degree program, title, professor, module, date), bibliography, plagiarism statement; Times New Roman or Calibri, 11–12pt, double-spaced; roughly 12–15 pages.
  • Revise with distance. Once you know what you actually want to say, go back and rewrite the introduction to match — and have someone else read it for clarity, philosopher or not.

docs.title: Handouts / Thesenpapiere (presentations & oral exams)
docs.text:
• Purpose: not a table of contents, not a full script — a compact set of claims you'll develop live.
  • Structure: header (name, DOB, matriculation number, degree program, module/seminar and instructor, date) → title/topic → one prose paragraph introducing the topic → 4–6 numbered theses → 3–4 references (≥1 primary, 1–2 secondary — only texts you actually used to prepare).
  • What counts as a thesis: a non-obvious, defensible claim — not a bare fact or a section-heading phrase. "Douglas argues that inductive risk makes non-epistemic values an ineliminable part of the scientific process" is a thesis; "The Value-Free Ideal" is not.
  • Formal requirements: 11–12pt, 1.5–2.0 spacing, max 2 pages, numbered theses, Chicago-style references. For an oral exam, send the handout at least 5 days ahead for review.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Ethical questions about AI, ordered roughly by time horizon. Near term: bias in algorithmic decision-making, privacy and surveillance, automation and unemployment. Mid term: governing increasingly autonomous systems (self-driving cars, autonomous weapons) and assigning responsibility for what they do. Long term: machine consciousness, moral status, and whether artificial agents could be owed moral consideration comparable to humans.

These are examined through utilitarian, deontological, virtue-ethical, and justice-based approaches, alongside principles such as harm prevention, fairness and non-discrimination, respect for autonomy, privacy, accountability, and moral status.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: What explains consciousness, and can philosophy or science explain it at all? The seminar compares attempts to explain mind, self, and subjective experience using philosophy, psychology, cognitive science, neuroscience, AI, literature, and science fiction. Topics: personal identity, self-consciousness, artificial intelligence, the mind–body relation, and whether consciousness could emerge from computation or complex information processing. The guiding question: what would count as an explanation of consciousness?

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Economics is also a deeply moral discipline. The seminar explores the interface of economics, ethics, and political philosophy: the moral foundations of markets, markets and freedom, the distribution of economic goods, and the moral limits of commodification. Guiding questions include whether market exchange is automatically legitimate, whether markets build or erode virtues, and how economic institutions shape our ideas of justice and the common good. Readings mix economists and philosophers.

docs.title: Learning goals
docs.text: By the end, students should be able to: know the core debates linking moral questions to markets; reconstruct their main concepts and positions; discuss them critically; and state their own position in speech and writing.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: How do ethical, social, and political values shape scientific research, and which of those influences are legitimate? The seminar moves from the value-free ideal, through the arguments from underdetermination and inductive risk and the distinction between direct and indirect roles for values, to recent debates on demarcating legitimate from illegitimate value influence, democratic legitimacy, partisan science, and proposals for a direct, even evidential, role for values.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
• Reconstruct the value-free ideal, separate its component claims, and explain why it came to be treated as common sense.
  • Characterize the arguments from underdetermination and from inductive risk and say how they differ.
  • Distinguish different roles values can play in science.
  • Assess proposals for telling legitimate from illegitimate value influences.
  • Evaluate recent proposals that values may play a direct or evidential role.
  • Apply these views to a case study from a scientific discipline.
